summary: Middle East oil-supply fears from the US-Iran conflict near the Strait of Hormuz are pushing energy costs and borrowing rates higher worldwide, forcing central banks from the Fed to the ECB, Banxico and the RBA to hold steady while investors flee to safe havens and pull back from riskier bets like crypto.
causalChain: Six days of US-Iran fighting near the Strait of Hormuz spiked oil prices and rattled global markets, pushing up inflation and borrowing costs from Germany to Mexico and prompting central banks everywhere to hold interest rates steady rather than risk fueling prices further. That same nervousness sent investors into safe-haven currencies like the yen and out of riskier bets like Bitcoin ETFs, while a separate shock -- China's breakthrough in making its own chipmaking tools -- hit Korean and Japanese tech stocks hard.

drafts.text: Oil slipped to about $90 a barrel Thursday, still far above last week, after jumping nearly 8% in one day, the biggest one-day jump in six years. Why: the US and Iran have attacked each other for six straight days near the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow strip of water between Iran and Arabia that about a fifth of the world's oil ships pass through daily. When tankers get hit there, oil buyers fear supply getting cut off, so they bid prices up, which means higher gas prices at the pump for drivers.

The Federal Reserve, the US central bank that sets how expensive it is to borrow money nationwide, voted 9 to 3 Wednesday to leave its rate unchanged at 3.5% to 3.75%. Three of its own officials wanted it raised instead, since prices have climbed faster than normal for five years, driven largely by costlier energy from the Middle East conflict. Keeping the rate steady means mortgages, car loans and credit cards stay about as pricey as now, instead of getting cheaper the way a rate cut would.

The interest rate the US government pays to borrow money for 30 years has stayed above 5% for most of July, the longest stretch since 2007. On July 9 the government sold $22 billion of this debt and had to offer a record 5.058% just to find buyers. That is happening because investors lending to the US are nervous about high oil prices, new import taxes, and the government borrowing huge sums year after year, so they demand more return, which then pushes up mortgage and business loan rates too.

The Mexican peso weakened to 17.46 per US dollar on Wednesday, down about a quarter of a percent in a day. Investors are nervous ahead of a big US Federal Reserve rate announcement, plus rising Middle East tension. Nervous investors pull money out of Mexico and buy dollars instead, seen as safer, and that extra buying makes the peso worth less. This means imported goods like gasoline cost a bit more for Mexicans, while dollars sent home by relatives in the US convert into slightly more pesos.

Mexico's statistics agency reported everyday prices were 3.10 percent higher in mid-July than a year earlier, down from 3.55 percent the month before. Prices are still rising, just more slowly. This happened mainly because fruit and vegetable prices fell, offsetting a small rise in fuel and utility costs. It matters because slower price increases give Mexico's central bank room to keep borrowing costs steady, or cut them later, without worrying cheaper loans will push prices up faster again.

Mexicans working abroad sent home 5.611 billion dollars in May, 3.8 percent more than a year earlier, a fourth straight month of growth. Fewer transfers were made, about 2 percent fewer, but each one averaged nearly 6 percent more money, at 404 dollars. This matters because millions of families in Mexico depend on cash from relatives in the US for food, rent, and school. A bigger total despite fewer transfers means senders send more each time, even as US jobs get harder to find for migrants.

Japan's currency, the yen, jumped 2% against the US dollar on July 30, its biggest one day gain since Japan's government stepped in to prop it up earlier this year. The yen had been sliding for weeks and neared its weakest level in 40 years, after Japan's central bank left interest rates unchanged this week instead of raising them again. When a currency falls that fast, investors bet the government will step in and buy yen to stop the slide, and that bet appears to have driven today's jump.

South Korea's stock market crashed more than 10% on July 28, one of its worst days ever, and Japan's stock market fell nearly 4% the same day. The trigger was news that a Chinese company had started making its own advanced chip making machines, tools that Korean and Japanese chip factories usually buy from a Dutch supplier. Investors sold Samsung and SK Hynix shares because China building this equipment itself threatens the technology edge those chip makers have relied on for years.

China's exports jumped 27% in June compared with a year earlier, the fastest growth in nearly five years and far above what economists expected. Factories shipped more goods abroad as companies rushed orders out ahead of new tariffs from other countries, and demand for Chinese made electronics stayed strong. Strong export numbers matter because they show how much money is flowing into China's economy from selling goods abroad, and they helped lift stock prices in Hong Kong this month.

The European Central Bank kept its main interest rate unchanged at 2.25 percent on July 23, choosing not to raise it again after increasing it in June, its first increase in three years. That June increase came after oil prices spiked when war broke out in the Middle East, since pricier oil makes fuel, heating, and shipping cost more, pushing up prices on nearly everything people buy. The bank is now watching to see how much further prices rise before deciding whether to raise rates again.

Germany's Adidas stock dropped 17 percent on July 30 after weaker than expected earnings, dragging Germany's main stock index, the DAX, down about half a percent. Meanwhile in Britain, the FTSE 100 stock index rose half a percent and sat near its highest level ever, lifted by the oil company Shell, which jumped after strong profits and a plan to buy back its own shares, and by Rolls-Royce, which climbed after raising its profit forecast for the year.

Germany's government statistics office said on July 30 that prices in July are expected to be 2.8 percent higher than a year ago, slightly more than the 2.7 percent economists predicted. The main driver is energy, with fuel and heating prices up over 8 percent from a year ago, largely because the Middle East conflict that began earlier this year pushed oil prices higher. Higher energy costs ripple through the economy, raising the price of transporting and making other goods too.

Australia's cost of living rose 3.8% over the year to June, down from 4.0% the month before, new data out this week showed. Housing was still the biggest driver, but the slowdown matters because Australia's central bank has kept interest rates high specifically to cool down price rises. Softer inflation makes it more likely policymakers hold rates steady at their next meeting in mid-August instead of raising them again, sparing households another jump in mortgage and loan costs.

Iron ore, used to make steel, fell this week to its lowest price in about three weeks. Chinese steel mills said stockpiles jumped 8% in one week, and warehouses at Chinese ports are fuller than usual too. That means factories already have plenty of ore on hand and are buying less new supply, a sign construction and steel output there are slowing. Australia sells huge volumes of iron ore to China, so weaker Chinese buying pulls down prices for Australian miners like BHP and Rio Tinto.

Workers at BHP's Port Hedland shipping terminal in Western Australia struck this month for the first time in 26 years, and pay talks remain unresolved. The dispute is about fairness: workers at BHP's nearby iron ore mines already got a 16% pay raise, but workers loading ships at the port did not, leaving pay gaps of up to 40,000 dollars a year for similar work. Port Hedland ships roughly 120 million dollars of iron ore daily, so a longer standoff could slow shipments to steelmakers in China.

Bitcoin's price slipped below $65,000 to about $63,100 this week after investment funds that let ordinary investors bet on Bitcoin's price saw $526 million pulled out over four straight days. When these funds sell Bitcoin to pay back investors cashing out, that selling adds pressure that pushes the price down further. Similar funds tied to Ethereum kept taking in new money instead, suggesting investors are shifting which currency they favor.

Ethereum's price broke above $1,820 and climbed toward $1,868 this week as large holders bought more coins and investment funds that let regular investors bet on Ethereum's price took in fresh money for a third straight week, reversing eight weeks of investors pulling cash out. Wallets holding between 1,000 and 10,000 coins grew from about 4,750 in early June to roughly 4,850 now, and when big holders and funds both buy at once, it tends to support higher prices.

The market for digital tokens designed to always be worth exactly one US dollar shrank for the first time in four years, with the largest of these tokens losing about $5.4 billion in value over sixty days, its biggest sustained drop outside a crisis. These tokens let traders move money quickly between exchanges without converting back to real bank dollars each time, so a shrinking supply means fewer dollars sitting ready in the trading system right now.

For the first time ever, scientists found real air around a rocky planet outside our solar system, sitting in the zone where liquid water could exist. The planet, LHS 1140 b, is 48 light-years away. Researchers spotted helium gas leaking from its upper atmosphere as starlight passed through it, proving the air has clung on for billions of years despite radiation blasts from its star. 📄 Published in Science · More: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/07/260721000825.htm

Astronomers caught an invisible black hole red-handed by watching a star wobble for over 20 years. A University of Utah team combined two decades of Hubble photos with new James Webb data to track a star tugged by something unseen, calculating a black hole about 4.5 times heavier than our sun. This cluster, Omega Centauri, is thought to hide 10,000 black holes, yet this is the first ever confirmed. 📄 Published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters · More: https://esahubble.org/news/heic2610/

Astronomers were not even looking for a new planet, and found one anyway. Two teams studying a well known planet in the Beta Pictoris system noticed something else glowing faintly inside the star's giant dust disk, a spot that had blocked every planet search there for over a decade. It turned out to be a new giant planet, twice as heavy as Jupiter, 63 light-years away. 📄 Published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters · More: https://www.mpia.de/news/science/2026-07-beta-pic-d

A colorful pet gecko might help scientists understand cancer. A rare golden yellow leopard gecko called lemon frost develops aggressive tumors in about 80 percent of individuals, and the same gene change behind its color also triggers the cancer. University of Nottingham researchers found these tumors share key genetic damage with human cancers, offering a new way to study cancer. 📄 Published in BMC Biology · More: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/07/260714225525.htm
